orders.objective:

field, each labelled with a lifecycle role; selects units as in a real-time
strategy game (click, shift-click, marquee, double-click for a squad, Escape

typed rows the decisions file names by id at activation, about ten in design

affordance); reads its five faces and parameters

steps reproduce the same frames; under reduced motion the field is still
until Step or Play; the canvas is a projection of a frame the text layer also
renders, and the renderer sits behind one interface so a 3D painter can
replace it later without touching the engine.

switchable to WO-226) as a strip of beats left to right in recorded time,
the distance between beats proportional to the minutes between rows; above

operator as a figure at the edge; stepping the anchor fills a slot with the

orders.title: WO-017 — The digital twin's first lane: the operator's patience after a hand-back as RxJS that runs on virtual time over the recorded WO-221, judged by the results of the order it would have run and never by agreement with the operator's beats, with every variant of the model kept as code and old versions never deleted
orders.objective:
at `/twin` the operator sees WO-221 as one time axis with its
sixteen beats as glyphs, a recorded lane carrying the operator's eight beats
as reference marks, and a twin lane carrying where the chosen variant of the
twin's patience stream fires after each hand-back when the order is replayed
on virtual time; the result cell beside the lanes states what the order would
have cost under the twin: the virtual close time, the twin's total waiting
minutes and the number of times it fired before anything was ready, each next

minutes; a variant picker lists every variant ever written with its version
and lineage, and a flip (a duration or a multiplier changed) redraws the twin
lane at once with a near-transparent ghost of the previous position and
recomputes the result cell; the operator saves a kept flip as a new variant
by exporting the TypeScript the UI generates, because the RxJS that describes
the operator is the RxJS that runs; the recorded lane never moves and no
agreement figure against it is computed or shown; WO-226 is the second order.

goalReview.goalStandard:
## Goal-aligned decisions

The [sequence](../planning/sequence.md) and selected work order determine
current placement and authority. The mission is the outcome; the critical path
is the dependency route to the next outcome. Useful prerequisite or
risk-reduction work must name the blocked outcome it enables. Process activity,
receipt volume and agent utilization are not progress by themselves. Goal
alignment grants no authority to reorder or expand work. In all phases, the Goal
Alignment and Process Cost procedure lives in the generated role skills
[WO-043, 2026-09-11].

Accuracy takes priority over agreement in every phase. The already-equipped
Correctness over Sycophancy rule applies to operator suggestions and the agent's
own premises equally: challenge unsupported claims, distinguish observation
from inference, state material uncertainty, and correct mistakes when evidence
changes. A confident request or an earlier decision is not proof of correctness.
Record material disagreement and its evidence in the same decision or phase
receipt; do not manufacture dissent or seek approval for ordinary judgment.

| Lens                                  | Decision question                                                                                         |
| ------------------------------------- | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| Policy resistance / fixes that fail   | Will local goals or guards undo one another?                                                              |
| Tragedy of the commons                | Does the solution consume shared compute, context or operator attention without accounting for the total? |
| Drift to low performance              | Does it improve an explicit outcome standard rather than normalize a worse baseline?                      |
| Escalation                            | Will additional process provoke more process or workarounds?                                              |
| Success to the successful             | Are credible alternatives excluded merely because the current mechanism already has investment?           |
| Shifting the burden to the intervenor | Does the solution remove recurring operator rescue or depend on it?                                       |
| Rule beating                          | Can the evidence pass without the intended behavior occurring?                                            |
| Seeking the wrong goal                | Does it advance operator flow and the selected product outcome rather than a proxy?                       |

Naive Interventionism adds the existing system's useful functions, affected
consumers, second-order harm, reversibility and smallest useful probe. NoOp
records what happens if nothing changes, why action or inaction wins, and the
evidence that would reopen the choice. Scale detail to consequence: explain
applicable risks and briefly group immaterial lenses with a reason; do not
manufacture eight repetitive paragraphs for routine edits.

Record evidence of benefit and the risks of intervening in existing behavior;
verification and handoff compare observed outcomes with the promised benefit.
Required legal or release actions retain their existing authority; NoOp is a
considered alternative, not an ambient veto or permission to abandon authorized
work.



Material choices and rationales go in existing phase evidence: per-order
`docs/evidence/WO-NNN/decisions.md` and cited product sections for work-order
decisions; planning dispositions/candidate records for planning choices; the
independent report or refutation receipt for its judgment; retained closeout
evidence for release decisions. The decisions index exposes per-order records.
Reuse and link a current rationale until its assumptions change; do not create
a parallel decision log or an extra approval ritual.


This launchpad is the operator's own DotLn instance. Its purpose is to plan and
run bounded, evidence-gated work orders across the operator's repositories, so
that every change arrives as a pull request the operator reads before it merges,
while the kit itself stays upstream and reaches this fork only through starter
updates. The first workstream is DotLn-Angular, an Nx and Angular monorepo that
serves two outcomes at once: the operator's reference Angular workspace, which a
colleague should recognize as the way the operator builds Angular, and the
operator's sandbox app, one app with sub-apps behind a menu: a scene for
authoring game AI from a toolbox mined from the works the operator reads, a
view of DotLn's machinery where a change to an agent's mechanisms shows what
changes in an example use case, the operator's own digital twin, and side
utilities. Every new idea lives there first as a toy the operator plays with
before promoting the ones that work, for the five UIFA roles, people and
software actors alike. The app is not wired to DotLn core: its data comes from
public mining into its own store, served to the UI through its own API, and it
informs the platform through GitHub issues, never by writing a control record,
so that the app improves the platform, the platform the starter, the starter
this fork, and the fork the app in turn. The critical path runs from registering
that repository in this launchpad, through one witnessed target order that
scaffolds the workspace, to a foundation where a feature is added by convention:
shared libraries, the component taxonomy, events and stores, the sub-app shell,
and a legitimate client-side authentication and permission model. Later
workstreams join the same way: one registration and one planning pass each,
with the fork's own machinery changes cut as self orders beside them.

episode.statement: I read exactly one file, the canonical refute prompt at <tmp>/scratch/refute-prompt.json, with the Read tool (one truncated read, then one complete read); I judged WO-015, WO-016, WO-008, WO-017 and WO-018 only from its compiled subject (the goal standard, the five cost-table trap observations, each order's title, objective, cost line, criteria and non-goals, the sequence, the empty deferrals and the cost table with its first verifications); the vision, the UIFA roles document, the capability table and the critical-path file were marked unavailable in the subject and I did not look for them; the session also carried harness-attached project instructions and a git status snapshot, which I did not use as evidence; I ran no shell command, searched nothing, opened no other file, spawned no agent and made no repository write or commit, and I wrote only result.json and statement.txt in the scratch refutation directory; the verdict is aligned-with-findings with no hold, because no supplied observation shows a failure of a judged order and the subject supplies no vision passage id.

orders.criticalPathAndNoOp: Gate: the vision passage names the sub-app shell as a foundation element, and WO-013 is that element. It unblocks WO-014 and WO-016, which declare hard dependencies on it, and through them WO-015, WO-017 and WO-018. It also settles WO-006-D005 (one app, sub-apps behind a menu). NoOp in the records: the cost-table row has metrics null. The observed gap is the NoOp state: one nav link, one BasePaths member, no sub-app. If nothing changes, every sub-app order has to invent its own route and menu placement. Action wins at a small cost (2 to 4 hours, about 24 files, no dependency). Its own hard dependency on WO-007 is not supported by its design (finding), so its place behind WO-007 is merge ordering, not a gate.
orders.systemTraps: Policy resistance: it respects the type:ui lint by keeping routerLink in app.ts and projecting the items into a template, so no guard is fought. Tragedy of the commons: the smallest order of the horizon. It adds one e2e spec (axe plus three viewport widths) and Storybook entries that every later gate reruns; otherwise immaterial. Drift to low performance: none. It adds a convention and keeps both the root redirect and the board route. Escalation: it adds two reference documents and a convention that every later sub-app order must follow and cite. Acceptable, because it replaces per-order invention. Success to the successful: a second app is rejected on the operator's recorded decision, and a router-owning menu is rejected on the lint axis. Credible. Shifting the burden: it assumes the operator accepts three group names, and there is no rescue path. Rule beating: criterion 6's grep for 'control record' passes on any sentence containing the phrase, including one that says the opposite. Low consequence, because review reads the file. Seeking the wrong goal: the three menu groups (Scene, Machinery, Tools) do not match the four sub-apps in the vision passage (scene, machinery view, digital twin, side utilities). The convention's 'sub-app' (a feature library) also differs from the objective's 'sub-app' (a menu group) (finding).
orders.removalBalance: No. It removes nothing: the board keeps its route and the bare link becomes the menu. It adds about 24 files, two libraries, two documents and a convention. Net additive by design; no process command is added.
orders.failureBehavior: Degrades. The root redirect and the board route are unchanged and asserted, so if scene or machinery fails to lazy-load, the old app is still reachable. The empty Tools group renders an empty-state line instead of a dead route. A navigation error reaches WO-007's error store through ErrorHandler. No refusal path is introduced.

findings.reason: The declared hard dependency on WO-007 cites 'the navigation store, the error surface and the persisted-state feature the shell and the arriving pages compose'. The design composes none of them: the menu template has no injection, the links stay routerLink in app.ts, and each arriving page has 'No facade, no store, no data'. The real coupling is file overlap, because WO-007 adds the notices container to libs/dotln/shell and app.ts. The stated reason is inaccurate, and it serializes a 2 to 4 hour order behind a 7 to 9 hour order even though the sequence format admits lane pairs.
findings.reopenWhen: WO-013's diff imports nothing from @dotln-angular/state, data-access or events, which would confirm the dependency is merge ordering only; or a later pass cites this dependency to block a lane pair.

findings.reason: 'Sub-app' names two different units. The objective calls the three menu groups sub-apps (Scene, Machinery, Tools), while the convention written into the two documents defines a sub-app as a feature library that exports routes. The vision passage lists four sub-apps: the scene, the machinery view, the operator's digital twin and side utilities. In this horizon the twin, a feature library with its own BasePaths member, is filed under the Machinery group (WO-017). The toolbox catalog and the toy shelf, which the vision ties to the scene, live under Tools, the side utilities. The convention documents will encode this ambiguity for every later sub-app to follow.
findings.reopenWhen: WO-017 adds /twin under the Machinery group and the operator asks for a twin group, or the 'how a sub-app is added' steps in sub-apps.md differ from the steps WO-014, WO-017 or WO-018 actually take.

orders.criticalPathAndNoOp: Gate: not a foundation element in the vision passage. It is the toolbox the vision's scene is authored from ('a toolbox mined from the works the operator reads'), so it is mission work, not a declared critical-path gate. It unblocks WO-015 (hard: the Tool types, the enum and the rail data) and WO-018 (hard: the schema, the layout, the check and the merge script). NoOp in the records: metrics null. The NoOp state is the observed gap: no catalog, no Tool type, rows only in core's ignored intake. If nothing changes, WO-015's rail has no typed tools and WO-018 has no pipeline. It is sequenced before WO-008 even though the vision names auth as a foundation element. Nothing in this order needs auth, and WO-008 covers every BasePaths member by type, so the delay to the foundation is a sequencing choice the operator owns, not a contradiction.
orders.systemTraps: Policy resistance: the allow-list is the clean-room rule made mechanical, and it is field-based over a whole directory. WO-018 later writes rows carrying the refused fields into that same directory (finding on WO-018). Tragedy of the commons: the most material trap here. The order itself calls the fan-out the largest spend of the workstream so far, with tokens unknown until run and recorded per worker, but sets no token ceiling and no stop rule. Twelve workers sit exactly at the cap, with no slack for the reruns step 7 requires (finding). About 3,500 data rows are bundled into the client. Drift to low performance: every row is classified once, while WO-015 consumes about 28 tools. Acceptable, since browsing the catalog is a stated outcome, but no first-batch probe is planned before all eight classifiers are dispatched. Escalation: two new commands, a check wired into check:fixtures and a rules document that later orders must obey; no check is retired. Success to the successful: an open transform string, a single worker, committing rows as they are, and loading over HTTP are each rejected with an axis. Credible. Shifting the burden: the executor disposes of the critic's findings; beyond the operator accepting the fan-out cost, the happy path has no operator rescue. Rule beating: criterion 3 is a quota (three typed tools per work across six works) that can pass by force-fitting concepts from PoEAA, GEB or Team Topologies into a closed enum built for units on terrain (finding). Criterion 5's statements that 'no quarantine file was read' are self-attested by the workers, although the harness journal could observe reads. Seeking the wrong goal: the order introduces a second data path (bundled JSON) beside the HTTP path WO-007 builds, while the vision passage says data is served through the app's own API (finding).
orders.removalBalance: No. It removes nothing. It adds about 40 source files, about 3,500 data rows, a schema, three scripts, two commands, a feature library, two documents and the largest subagent spend of the workstream. The addition is the deliverable.
orders.failureBehavior: Mostly correct refusals, plus one unspecified path. A drifted map count fails criterion 1 loudly; the order treats a changed count as a decision, never a silent renumbering. A failing sampled tool reruns only its own batch, because the checkpoint is the unit of rerun. An untyped row is browsable but never executable, which degrades rather than refuses. Unspecified: what /tools/catalog shows when a lazy chunk import fails; no error or empty state is named for CatalogLoader.

findings.reason: This order creates a second data path. WO-007 moves even the one recorded board document behind the app's own API, over HTTP answered by MSW. WO-014 instead bundles about 3,500 catalog rows as lazy JSON chunks through CatalogLoader's import(), and WO-015 to WO-018 follow with bundled fixtures and data. The loader seam mitigates this for the catalog, but the horizon ends with two paths and no stated rule for choosing between them. The vision passage says the app's data is 'served to the UI through its own API'. In production, the bundled sub-apps work and the HTTP board does not.
findings.reopenWhen: Candidate C1 is cut and has to change more than CatalogLoader and WO-016's fixture pack (for example, a feature imports a data file directly), or a later order adds a third data path.

findings.reason: The worker plan has no slack. Eight classifiers, two sampling checkers, one synthesizer and one critic make twelve, which is exactly the cap criterion 5 enforces. Step 7 requires rerunning the classifier on every failing id a checker returns. A rerun spawned as a new worker makes thirteen and fails criterion 5. That pushes the executor to skip reruns, or to resume workers in a way the evidence README does not record separately.
findings.reopenWhen: Either sampling checker returns at least one failing id, or the evidence README lists a rerun dispatch.

findings.reason: Criterion 3 is a quota: three tools with a closed-enum transform for each of six works, including PoEAA, GEB and Team Topologies. The enum's fourteen kinds cover steering, formation, squads, channels, ground and levels. The criterion can pass by force-fitting a transform onto a concept that has none. The only counter-pressure is the checkers' sample asking whether the transform is observable in a twenty-unit scene, and WO-015's rail then presents those tools as executable.
findings.reopenWhen: A checker or the critic disputes any of the eighteen first-three tools, or a work's first three carry a transform kind that WO-015's engine does not interpret.
